summary: When an emergency call reaches a Public Safety Answering Point, the device, access network and service providers may hold helpful information about the call, caller or location. This standards-track RFC describes data structures and mechanisms to convey such additional data to the PSAP.

eli5.summary: When you call for help, the phone and network can pass along extra useful facts. This defines how.

questions: additional data related to an emergency call

subtitle: A common set of data blocks that devices and providers can attach to an emergency call, by value or by reference.

tldr.problem: When an emergency call reaches a Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP), the device, the access network and the service providers hold helpful information about the call, the caller or the location, but there was no common way to hand it over.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines five XML data blocks, each with its own MIME media type, and two ways to carry them: a SIP Call-Info header pointing to a block, or the provided-by element of a PIDF-LO location object. Either way, a block travels by value or by reference.
tldr.outcome: Every emergency call is meant to carry as much of this data as possible. The data is sensitive, so the RFC requires HTTPS with mutual authentication for blocks sent by reference and discusses privacy at length.

today: RFC 7852 is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 6443 and RFC 6881, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Extra Facts for the Emergency Call Taker
sections.content:
An IP-based emergency call already carries identity, device capabilities, location and more to the PSAP. RFC 7852 extends the basic data set described in RFC 6443 and RFC 6881 with additional data that the device, the access network provider and each service provider in the call path hold. The intent is that every emergency call carry as much of it as possible.

The RFC sorts additional data into three categories: data associated with a location (such as floor plans), with a call (provider, service, device and subscriber details) and with a caller (such as medical information). It defines structures only for the call category, but it builds the framework, transport and registries so other documents can add the rest.

The scope is limited to emergency calls. The data is private, so it is not appropriate for ordinary calls. The one stated exception is a private arrangement, such as a vehicle telematics provider and its in-vehicle equipment, where the endpoints already have a relationship that handles privacy.
sections.eli5: When someone calls for help, the phone company and the phone itself know useful things, like what kind of phone it is. This lets them pass those facts to the person answering.

sections.title: The Five Data Blocks
sections.content:
Each data structure is a block: an XML document with its own MIME media type. The five blocks are Data Provider, Service Information, Device Information, Owner/Subscriber and Comment. Every block must contain a <DataProviderReference> element. Its value has the syntax of an RFC 5322 Message-ID, without the angle brackets, and must be world-unique. All blocks that one entity adds at the same time MUST carry the same value, which ties them together as a unit.

The Data Provider block says who supplied the data. Any entity that provides any other block MUST supply it. It carries a display string and a provider ID, plus the ID series that says who issued the ID: NENA, EENA or domain. A US provider registered with NENA MUST use its NENA Company ID in the form urn:nena:companyid:<ID>. The block also has a required provider type (for example Telecom Provider, Access Network Provider or Telematics Provider) and a required contact URI. For a service or access provider this URI is a 24/7 support contact, preferably a tel URI in E.164 format. The RFC says PSAPs do not use it for callbacks. Optional parts include supported languages, an xCard and, for subcontractors, who they work for and whom to call first (sub or main).

Reusing the vCard format for contact details, the RFC adds a main-number value for the TYPE parameter of a tel property, because a vCard has no way to mark an enterprise's main number, which responders find useful.
sections.eli5: Each fact sheet is a form with a name tag on it, so the call taker knows who filled it out and how to reach them if something is unclear.

sections.title: Service, Device, Subscriber and Comment Details
sections.content:
The Service Information block describes the service the caller has. ServiceType is required and can have several values; the initial registry includes wireless, coin, POTS, OTT, MLTS-hosted, MLTS-local, sensor-attended, sensor-unattended and relay. ServiceMobility is required and is one of Mobile, Fixed, Nomadic or Unknown. ServiceEnvironment (Business, Residence or Unknown) is required unless the service type is wireless. The RFC calls this advisory information: it reflects the provider's best knowledge, not the true character of the premises.

The Device Information block describes the device, not how it is used. Optional elements are a device classification (for example cordless, smart-phone or automobile), manufacturer, model number and a unique device ID with a type attribute such as IMEI, MAC or SN. It can also carry a URI to device-specific data plus a type; the only initial type is IEEE1512. The RFC says call takers will probably not use manufacturer, model or ID, but PSAP management might in an investigation.

The Owner/Subscriber block holds an xCard for the owner or subscriber and a required privacyRequested boolean. The RFC leaves the meaning of that flag to the receiving jurisdiction. The contact address is a nominal one, not necessarily the caller's location. The Comment block is free human-readable text for PSAP staff and is not meant as a general extension mechanism.
sections.eli5: The other forms say what kind of phone service it is, what kind of phone, who owns the phone, and any extra note. Some forms are only helpful if you need to investigate later.

sections.title: Adding New Kinds of Data
sections.content:
There are two ways to add new data: define a new block, or define a new type for the device-specific data URI in the Device Information block. The RFC warns that the real obstacle is not the format. PSAPs and responders need software upgrades and training before they use new data, and legal and operational review may be needed. Overwhelming call takers with too much information is highly discouraged, so the barrier to supporting new data is described as quite high.

The choice between the two ways depends on four things. Information many device kinds will send fits better as a separate block. Data sent through the Device Information URI goes by reference, which adds some privacy protection because the requester must supply a verified certificate. Very large data suits that reference route, small data suits a block sent by value. A block can be sent by value without a server, while the reference route needs one.

The RFC encourages widely shared formats for each class of device, because variations, however well intentioned, are unlikely to be supported.
sections.eli5: Anyone can invent a new form, but the people answering calls need training to use it. So the rule is to agree on one form for everyone instead of making many.

sections.title: Carrying Blocks in SIP and PIDF-LO
sections.content:
Two transports are defined. The first uses the SIP Call-Info header field with a new purpose value that starts with EmergencyCallData, a dot, and the block type, such as EmergencyCallData.ProviderInfo. The header holds either an HTTPS URL (data by reference) or a cid: URI that points to a MIME body part in the same message (data by value). A reference MUST be an HTTPS URI, so TLS protects retrieval. Several body parts travel in multipart/mixed, and since proxies may not change bodies, an entity adding a block by value needs a suitable SIP element such as a back-to-back user agent.

At least one such Call-Info MUST be present. A device MUST provide one unless it knows a service provider is in the path, and each service provider in the path MUST insert its own. This header has meaning only in an emergency call, a test emergency call or a private arrangement with an existing relationship.

The second transport is for the access network provider, which cannot add a Call-Info header because it does not take part in the application signaling but can supply a PIDF-LO location object. It uses the <provided-by> element, with <EmergencyCallDataReference> (attributes ref and purpose) for references and <EmergencyCallDataValue> to embed blocks. The RFC recommends access networks send by reference, because PIDF-LOs can be fetched and stored by others, so by-value data risks wider exposure.

Only blocks in the registry may be sent this way, and each entity that adds data MUST include a Data Provider block. If a block is malformed or of the wrong type, the general principle is that it is more important for the call to go through than for everything to be correct.
sections.eli5: The call can carry the facts inside the envelope, or just a link telling where to get them. Links are safer because only people with the right badge can open them.

sections.title: Security of Additional Data
sections.content:
These structures hold information usually considered private. Data sent by value is visible to SIP proxies, back-to-back user agents and anyone able to eavesdrop on the signaling, so TLS 1.2 or later SHOULD be used when feasible. This is not a MUST because deployed clear-text SIP exists and because the call MUST proceed even if TLS negotiation or certificate verification fails.

For data by reference the rules are stricter. TLS mutual authentication is REQUIRED: HTTPS is needed, the requester MUST use a client certificate and the provider MUST validate it. TLS MUST be version 1.2 or later, and the RFC recommends cipher suites with Perfect Forward Secrecy that avoid CBC, following BCP 195 (RFC 7525). PSAPs and responders are strongly advised to deploy a PKI so data providers can check the requester's certificate. No global mechanism for distributing the root credentials exists yet, so data providers may need to get them out of band.

Devices are generally not expected to provide data directly by reference. They would normally send by value or upload the data to a server. Neither devices nor providers will supply private data unless the call is recognized as an emergency call, so providers of cellular service ought to reject a misdialed emergency call with the code that makes the device retry as an emergency call.
sections.eli5: These facts are private, so the link version needs a proper ID check before anyone can read them. If the check fails during a real emergency, though, the call still goes through.

sections.title: Privacy Trade-offs
sections.content:
The data goes far beyond what the legacy telephone system shared. Data protection rules in many places make exceptions for emergencies, because the benefit to the caller outweighs the harm of disclosure, though some countries still offer callers a degree of anonymity toward call takers. The explicit privacy indicator in the Owner/Subscriber block is mandatory to include, but whether it is honored is up to the destination jurisdiction.

The RFC lists the privacy threats it considers, based on RFC 6973: stored data compromise, misattribution, identification, secondary use and disclosure. It notes that emergency services are often obliged to keep call data for extended periods, which raises the risk of breaches. Where callers can suppress identifying information, networks or PSAPs can inspect SIP privacy flags, such as the id priv-value of RFC 3325, to decide what to pass on or display.

Because data by value is visible to every intermediary, sending by reference may be more appropriate for sensitive data, but only if the provider can run a dereferencing service with access control. Without access control, anyone holding the reference can resolve it.
sections.eli5: Sharing more facts helps the helpers but also means more private details are floating around. So the rules say to keep them safe and use them only for emergencies.

sections.title: Registries and Media Types
sections.content:
The RFC creates an "Emergency Call Additional Data" registry with nine sub-registries: Provider ID Series, Service Environment, Service Type, Service Mobility, Type of Provider, Device Classification, Device ID Type, Device/Service Data Type and Emergency Call Data Types. Most use Expert Review. The last two use the stricter Specification Required, which includes expert review, because the RFC wants to be conservative about registering new data.

In the Emergency Call Data Types registry, each block is identified by the root of its MIME subtype, the part after EmergencyCallData.. A subtype that does not start with that prefix cannot be registered or used in a Call-Info header as this RFC specifies. IANA also registers the EmergencyCallData purpose parameter value, five MIME types of the form application/EmergencyCallData.*+xml, XML namespaces and schemas, a URN for the provided-by element and the vCard main-number value.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of every kind of form that is allowed. New forms have to be checked and added to the list before anyone can use them.
